Based on the foregoing, when you wrote the Department, you still have no copy Of the Sandiganbayan Decision. Per our records at that time, the Department has not yet received a copy thereof. Hence, in a letter dated 30 April 2014, we wrote Atty. Estela Teresita C. Rosete, Executive Clerk of Court, Sandiganbayan (1st Division) requesting for a copy of the Decision rendered by the Sandiganbayan (1st Division) in Criminal Case No. 28328. On 09 Vlay 2014, we received the 07 May 2014 letter-reply from Atty. Rosete, which reads: ' This responds to your letter dated April 30, 2014 concerning the above-captioned case. The decision there was promulgated on January 30, 2014, in which this Court convicted accused Cornelio C. Martinez, Jr., Eugene L Alzate, Lilebeth L CaniIIo-Prospero, Hernando L. Sibugan, Juanito H. Accused Abate, Abiso, Sibugan, Marcelo, Martinez, Desedilla and CaniHo-Prospero filed their separate motions for reconsideration. In a promulgated on May 5, 2014, the court resolved the motions (among other related matters), denying the motions except that of Cornelio C. Ma ez, Jr. who was therein acq uitted. Accused Purisima and Zoleta did not move for reconsideration of the Decision. As requested, we are attaching hereto copies of the above- mentioned Decision and Resolution for your ready reference. " Per our recent verification with our Provincial Director in Sarangani, the Decision rendered by the Sandiganbayan (1st Division) in Criminal Case No. 28328 is on appeal with the Suprenle Court. We also verified with the Sandiganbayan and according to the 1st Division, the records of thescase are already with the Supreme Court as of this date. Since your queries pertain to the same subject matter, we nevertheless deem It proper to answer, in seriatim, the queries enumerated in the letter of Vice-Governor Pacquiao since Äey are more exhaustive.

Whome- a. not the public officials are still considere, ' Board Members? I.e. be noted that the accused in Criminal Case No. 28328 are Cornelio C. Desedilla (former Sangguniang Panlalawigan Members), and Amelia Constantino-Zoleta (former executive assistant). As alrea y mentioned in our recital of facts, our Provincial Director in Sarang-am: confirmed that the Decision rendered by the Sandiganbayan (ISt Division) in Criminal Case No. 28328 is presently on appeal with the Supreme Court. Since accused Martinez was acquitted cn the ground of reasonable doubt in the Resolution promulgated on 05 May 2012 the Sandiganbayan (1st Division) so that, to date, he was already released from custody of the Bureau of Corrections, accused Alzate is therefore the only local elective who might have taken such appeal before the Supreme Court. In e, 12gard, in People of the Philippines vs. Jalosjosl, the Supreme Court Banc) ve quote: ' 'Y-xx the Aguihaldo case involves the administrative removal of a public ouncer for acts done prior to his present term of office. It does not apply to imprisonment arising from the enforcement of criminal law. Moreover, in the same way that preventive suspension is not removal, confine ? ent pending appeal is not removal. He (lalosjos) remains a congress-nan unless expelled by Congress or. otherwise. disqualified. " (Empha is Supplied) Based on the foregoing, an elective official who is confined during the pendency of his aplYA should not be considered removed from such office, unless expelled or otherwise d Vqulified. therefore the foregoing to the herein case of accused Alzate, his confinemen the National Bilibid Prison should not be construed as removal from'lils position as Sangguniang Panlalawigan Mem ber, unless otherwise disqualified2. 1 G.R. No. 132875-76 dated 03 February 2000. 2 Let it be noted the power to expel members of the sanggunian for disorderly behavior is opined to be for that particular session only (DILG Opinion 83, series of 2004)---fthe Sanggunian cannot 'dismiss' their colleague for breach of internal discipline taking into account that the allowable, disciplinary sanctions for such breach is only suspension or expulsi( •n. e i ofa ber for disorderly behe_yior. Airthermore, since the ground relied upon by the sanggunian barangay is neither of the two grounds within which a Sanggunian may internally discipline its members, the misconduct allegedly committed by the barangay kagawad .1»es not fall within the ambit of Section 50 (b) (5) of RA 7160. At most, the alleged misconduct should have been proper subject of an administrative complaint based on Section filed before the Sangguniang Panlungsod oi Quevzon City pursuant to Sec. 61(c) both of RA 7160. Therefore, the sanggunian barangay concerned exceeded its power when it imposed a penalty on the barangay kagawad based on an alleged attempted bribery." (Emphasis

b. Wh - or not they are still allowed to receive salary and representation allowance? While il may be true, as discussed above, that an elective official confined durmg the pendency o ? his appeal should not be considered removed from such office, unless otherwise disqudified, we are of the view that accused Alzate can no longer receive his salaries and rep •esentation and transportation allowance (RATA) during such period of his incarceration. In Peop e of the Philippines vs. Maceda, et al.3, the Supreme Court held: 'As a matter of law, when a person indicted for an offense is arvesl?ü, he is deemed placed under the custody of the law. He is placed in aa - .vu cestraint of liberty in jail so that he may be bound to answer for the commission of the offense. He must be detained in jail during the pendency of the case against him, unless he is authorized by the court to be releasea' on bail or on recognizance. Let it be stressed that all prisoners whether_ under preventive detention or serving final sentence can not practice _ their profession nor engage ip any business or occupation* or hold office. e ective or a inti while in deten •on. is a n consequence of arresr and detention. Through [an] interdepartment coordination, he is also provided with an office at the Administration Building New Bilibid Prison, Muntinlupa City, where he attends to his constituents. " Accused-appellant further admits that while under detention, he has filed several bills and resolutions. It also appears that he has been receiving his salaries and other monetary benefits. Succinctly stated, accused-appellant has been discharging his mandate as a member of the House of Representative consistent with the restraints upon one who is presenml.y• under detention. Being a detainee, accused-appellant should not been allowed by the prison authorities at the National to perform these acts. " (Emphasis Supplied) G.R. No. 89591-96, 24 January 2000. 4 Supra.

Let it be noted that a salary is defined by the Supreme Court in Santiago vs. COAS as something 'tcxx received as a matter of right in recompense for services rendered" (Emphasis Supplied). On the other hand, in the case of RAT A, Item 7.5 of the Local Budget Circular:No. 1036 dated 15 May 2013 is instructive, thus: "7.5 For officials who, by the nature of their official functions, adopt a work schedule other than the usual eight hours per day, forty hours week, such as the members of the local sanggunian. RA TA shall pro-rated based on the actual work/attendance of the official vis the work schedule or performance standards prescribed by law xxx" (Emphasis Supplied) Since the accused official is presently detained and as such cannot render actuål work/attendance in the Sangguniang Panlalawigan, it follows that he is not also entitled to receive both lis salary and RATA covering the period of his confinement. Wheth:r or not they can still enjoy the benefits appurtenant to their being as peb!ic• officials, such as to use their leave cma'its, if they can, what will be the neccee o/ their leave? Section 81 of the Local Government Code of 1991 (RA 7160) and CSC Memorandum '&ircular No. 41 Series of 1998, as amended by Memorandum Circular No. 14 series of 199! , Section 5, reads: "SECTI N 5. Leave credits of local elective officials. Said leave credits shall be commutative and cumulative. If his confinement, the accused official has already accumulated or earneul leave credits, yve are of the view that he may use the same while under confinement. In this regard, it may be worthy to note the decision of the Supreme Court in Agustina M. Enemicio vs. Office of the Ombudsman, et. al.7 adopting the ratiocination of the Office of the Ombudsman. Melencion, Vocational School Superintendent. All these leaves pay indicating that the respondent availed of his leave credits undeniably due to him by law. It matters not how the respondent utilizes the days where he is on leave. be they enjoyed as a vacation_ or. in this case. incarceration for a crime. There appears to be no regulation or law against the utilization of leave credits for purposes other than recu eation. xxx" (Emphasis Supplied) d. As to the staffs under their supervision, will they be automatically reporting [o the Office of the Vice Governor us tife appointing authority or can the •zamed Board Members still instruct thc.'i: staffs to do regular routinary works c,Mduct official travels with their recommendation (their signatures will appear jn the travel order as recommendation for the approval of the Vice-Governor); We reply both in the negative. As discussed above, confinement prevents the accused elective official from performing his duties and functions as such. Along this line, it was also reiterated that confinement by an elective official is not removal. Removal from office is one of the grounds gi e rise to a permanent vacancy under Section 448 of the Republic Act No. 7160 or the Government of 1991. confinement in jail may only be considered as a temporary incapacity which gives rise to temporary vacancy in an elective office under Section 46 of the Local Government Ccde of 1991. Let it be noted that a temporary incapacity which gives rise to temporary v icancy in an elective office under the aforesaid provision of the Local Government Ccde of 1991 may be due to physical or legal reasons such as, but not limited leave of absence, travel abroad, and suspension from office. Regrettably, the Local Government Code of 1991 is silent on the mode of succession in the event of a temporary vacancy in the Office of the Vice-Governor and in 8 SECTION 44. nent Vacancies in the Offices of the Governor, Vice-Governor, Mayor, and Vice-Mayor---xxx For purpose of this Chapter, a permanent vacancy arises when an elective official fills a higher vacant office, refuses to assu.ne OIEce, fails to qualify, dies, is removed from office, voluntarily resigns, or is otherwise permanently incapacitated u_» disc n ge the functions of his office

the Sanggunian However, the silence of the law must not be understood to convey that a remedy in law is wanting. In order to obviate the dilemma resulting from an interregnum created by the •vacancy, the mode for filling-up of permanent vacancies in the sanggunian set forth under Section 45 of the Local Government Code of 1991 shall be applied9. The sanggunian member who filled-up the position of SP Member Alzate shall discharge the duties and functions of the latter until his temporary incapacity exists. e. • or not they can still propose measures before the Sangguniang Pamala wigan? W? already answered this issue in letter b. f. Will there be a legal justification if they will four (4) consecutive absences during sessions?; We ansver in the affirmative. Section (b)(5) of the Local Government Code of 1991 provides and we quote: 5) The discipline of members for disorderly behavior and absences cause for four (4) consecutive sessions, for which they my be censured, reprimanded, or excluded from the session, suspended for not *nore than sixty (60) days, or expelled: Provided, That the penalty of suspension or expulsion shall require the concurrence ofat least two-thirds (2/3) vete of all the sanggunian members: Provided, further, That a membe}• convicted by final judgment to imprisonment of at least one (I) year for any crime involving moral turpitude shall be automatically expelled form the sanggunian; and" (Emphasis Supplied) We reiterate that the confinement of SP Member Alzate prevents him from performing his duties and functions, including his attendance to the regular sessions conducted by the Sangguniang Panlalawigan. Such confinement may thus be considered as a justifiable. cause for SP Member Abate not to attend the regular sessions, hence, this would reader the aforequoted provision of the Local Government Code of 1991 inapplicab:e to his case. 9 G.R. No. 90762, 20 1991.

Upon receipt of the order and/or copy of the dec:sion of the Sandiganbayan, will it be immediately executory even pending motion for reconsideration/appeal to be taken by C. he Board Members? Our Provincial Director in Sarangani confirmed that the Decision rendered by the Sandiganbayan (1st Division) in Criminal Case No. 28328 is presently on appeal with the Supreme Ct. In Lubrica vs. People of the Philippines10, the Supreme Court had an occasion to pass upon the effect of an appeal taken on the decisions and final orders of the Sandiganbayan thus: tion 7 of Presidential Decree 1606 as amended b Re ub1icAc 8249. p vides Chat 'decisions and final orders of the Sandiganbayan shall be_appealable to the Supreme Court by petition for resQvv on certiorari questions of law in accordance With rule 45 of the Rules of Cev=re__ The said rule provides 15 days from notice of the denial of his motion_for reconsideration within which to file a petition for review. an appea/, the judgment becomes final upon expiration of the peri; execution should necessarily follow. Y-.rere, petitioner failed to comply with the proper procedure. Instead M a petition for review on certiorari to this Court within the reglementary period, he submitted a notice of appeal months after the judgment had attainec) finality. Not only did he act belatedly, petitioner also resorted to the wrong mode of appeal. Thus. petitioner's notice Qf no legal effect and cannot suspend the enforceme/lt of hié sentence The argument is untenable. ule 122 of the Rules ofCourt gives the effect of an appeal taken by one or nore of the several accused: SEC. 11. Effect of appeal by any of several accused. — (b) An appeal taken by on e or m ore of several accused shall not affect those who did not appeal, except insofar as the judgment is fa vorable and applicable to the latter. From the foregoing, it is clear that the appeals taken by co-accused Baldera•na and Nagal cannot help petitioner insofar as suspension of execution is concerneå. The benefit of stay of execution afforded to a co- 10 G.R. Nos. 156147-54 dated 26 February 2007.

accused vho timely files an appeal cannot be extended to those who failed to file zoesame Thus, the period to appeal continued to run against petiticner notwithstanding the petition for review filed by his co-accused.
